That covers most of it. One gap still decides the overall shape of the tool: the device you log on.

**Where do you want to type contacts as they happen, especially at field days with no internet?**

- **A. A laptop.** A desktop program or a command-line tool that runs locally.
- **B. A phone or tablet.** An app that saves contacts on the device and syncs later.
- **C. Both.** For example, a phone at field days and a laptop at home, with one shared log.
- **D. Paper stays at the station.** You keep the notebook and want faster entry afterwards, not live logging.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- With no internet at field days, the log must save to local storage first. A cloud-only web app fails at exactly the moment you need it.
- Option C is the costly one. Two devices that each edit the log offline need a merge rule for when they reconnect. That adds a lot of work, so it helps to know early whether you really need it.
- ADIF (Amateur Data Interchange Format, the plain-text log format that Logbook of The World accepts) is simple to write. The choice of device will shape the design much more than the export will.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`
